name: Agentic Drafting and Multi-Model Workflows
title: Agentic Drafting and Multi-Model Workflows
answer: Agentic drafting and multi-model workflows cover the use of AI systems that do more than answer a single prompt. In literary arts and narrative design, this means giving an agent a goal such as draft a chapter, revise a scene for tone, or check a manuscript for continuity, and letting it plan steps, call different models, and return a finished piece. The scope includes long-form fiction, interactive dialogue trees, game narrative bibles, and serialized prose where consistency across many scenes matters. It also covers the coordination of multiple models, each chosen for a different narrative task, rather than relying on one general-purpose model.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These workflows run on orchestration software that sits between the writer and the models. The orchestration layer sends prompts to hosted model APIs or local inference servers, stores intermediate drafts, and passes relevant context such as character sheets or prior chapters into each model call. Many setups use a vector database or a simple project file to hold the story bible, so agents can retrieve only the lore they need for a given scene. The infrastructure does not require a machine learning engineer, but it does require some comfort with scripting, API keys, and structured prompts.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is usually done as a loop. A planner agent breaks the task into smaller steps, a writer agent produces a draft, a critic agent checks it against the story bible or style guide, and an editor agent applies revisions. Different models are assigned by strength: one model may handle natural dialogue, another may be better at factual or timeline consistency, and a third may polish prose. The human writer sets the goal, reviews each stage, and decides which agent outputs to keep, so the final text remains a collaboration rather than a single black-box generation.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk are unsettled. The provenance of each passage matters, so working methods should log which model produced which text, what prompt was used, and what source material was retrieved. Publishers and platforms may require disclosure of AI assistance, and contracts may treat AI-generated prose differently from human-written prose. There is also a risk that a model reproduces memorized phrases or closely imitates a living author's style, which can lead to infringement claims. Keeping a clear record of human edits and agent outputs is the most practical safeguard.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward persistent agent teams that maintain a living story bible across an entire series or game. Agents will likely handle longer-horizon tasks such as tracking character arcs, flagging contradictions, and suggesting revisions that respect earlier choices. Multi-model workflows will become more common as writers mix specialized models for dialogue, description, and plot logic. The human role will shift further toward direction and taste, while the agents handle the mechanical drafting and continuity checks.
